Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. And he beat the same, how about the blues? He wouldn't beat the blues? The blues numbers, well no, some of the blues numbers he used to play on this order.
Oh yeah, so he played the same beat every whatever he was playing, the same beat.
That's the experience I had with him, yeah.
Well, when was it that you saw him playing like that? What year?
That was in the year of 1919 at the Old Lyric Theatre.
Oh yeah, was that with the Robichaux band?
John Robichaux's band at the Old Lyric Theatre.
You remember who else was in that band at that time?

It was, so far I can remember it was John Robichaux was the violin and the leader. They had a lady by the name of Miss Kimmel and her husband was a trumpet player. And I think, let's see, it was Alphonse Picou playing the clarinet. No, it was old man Charlie McCurtis.
Oh yeah.
I think it was old man Kimmel on the bass violin. Oh, Henry Kimmel. Henry Kimmel. Well, all regular numbers from the, during the show days. I couldn't think of all of them by the name at present.
But it was, let's see, the shows used to come in once a week.

Like some shows, it was last two weeks, some of them last one of the vaultables. They played all for the vaultables. They played all for the vaultables shows. And then they had, I think it was, let's see, some of them, I know they use high society a lot. Oh yeah, yeah. They use for the overture. Yeah. High society. High society. Yeah. Because Pickle would make with that tune. Yeah. That was Pickle's tune. Yeah. They had a fellow by the name of, he's a trombone player by the name of, that man's name again,
he was Johnny Lindsay.

Oh, Johnny Lindsay. Johnny Lindsay, yeah. Johnny Lindsay, the trombone player, yeah. He was playing the trombone. Where did Red Happy go after that band? Do you remember where he went? Let me see. Red Happy stood a good while with the lyric, with the John Robichoux band. I'm not mistaken. I believe he went from the band.
Yeah.
He went from the band. Yeah. He went from the band. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And after he left the band, he went to Chicago. Chicago. Illinois. Yeah. He went to Chicago, and he stood up there a good while. I believe till he died.
I believe he used to sing vocals in that with the band.

He did some medium. I don't know about him singing in all this. He did lots of comedy work on the stage too, you see. I don't know if he ever, I never did see him play while the band, I mean sing while the band was playing. Most likely they'd be playing for the vaudeville show, you see. go there regular to watch the play? I used to sit right down in that time they called it the orchestra. Yeah, yeah. We used to call that, it was all colored show theater, you see, I used to sit right behind the band. What kind of a drum set did he have, drum outfit, you know, what kind? Oh, all I can remember was there was a yellow looking bass drum. I wouldn't know the name of it, you know what I mean? And four carbells, small side tum-tums, and the rattlers and the regular crash cymbals, and he was a very fast acted drummer. Two cymbals he had? I don't remember two cymbals. I know he had the old time crash cymbals with the side cymbals on the side of
the bass drum. How would those cymbals work on the bass drum? Well, they work, you see,

you had a beater, you had the overhead beaters on the bass drum, and you had like a hammer on the side of it. You could release it, you know, when you want to play the bass drum without hitting that side cymbal, you just could take your stick and raise that lever up, you see, it was working this motion like this, and you could take your sand and just raise it up, and you wouldn't hit the cymbal. But it hit exactly the same time? Same time with the beater, with your bass drum ball, yeah. They both hit the same time, and playing, if you want to release that, and your overheads used to fasten the top of your bass drum, and with a spring, make the spring actions, and you had to the flow, you used to have a pedal, a wooden pedal, and you fasten that again, the ball used to work over on this motion, like from overhead, and then you had a strap down, it used to meet the foot pedal, you see, and then they used to work it that way. Then you could have your cymbal always to your right of your bass, and you'd be sitting and you'd, similar like this, this mute on this bass drum now. And when you beat, otherwise the bass beat the ball in the, that hammer used to hit the cymbal at the same
time, same beat here. So, and then you'd let, you let it off for the softer passages, would
you, this thing? Yeah, yeah, you'd just release it for softer passages, that's right, yeah.
Yeah. Do you remember any other drummers of that time? You can remember any, had any specific beats in there? Uh-oh.
Well, Happy was the, let's see, well we had Chani, we all called him Chani Bebe.
Oh yeah.
He was a famous drummer with the original Tuxedo Band. Abbie Foster was his right name. We all called him Chani Bebe.
What kind of stuff did he play? You remember anything?

He was another special. His style of drumming was almost similar to Happy's style. He was a great snare drum player, man, too. He was a great snare drum. And the most drummer, the best snare drum player we had in New Orleans was Louis Contrell.
Oh yeah, yeah.
Louis Contrell, he was raised as the best in handling the snies. In fact, he taught drums.
Did you ever see that folding drum he had?
Yeah, the collapsible. What was that like, that collapsible? Well, it was one of the reminders, the way they used to fold it, they had a case similar like the old-time baritone saxophone case.
Yeah.
And used to dampen it. When you dampen the head, you always had to put a piece of newspaper when you dampen it, and to stop the head from getting dry rot.
Oh yeah.

See, every time you close the bass drum, you take a piece of newspaper and you dampen it, and you put it between the seam of the drum, then you fold it over. Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. It's like you do a seal.
Yeah.
Then you stick. But the case of the bass drum looked just like a baritone cypher. It was like a steeple, like a humpback to it.
It was the actual drum, bass drum that folded up small.

Yeah, it folded, yeah. It took plenty of time to rig it up, but it was not quite wide as this bass drum. After it'd be folded, I figured this would be about the width of about 12, 1 foot, 12 inches after it'd be rigged up. Yeah. You understand? It'd be about 1 foot.
And then that would fold up and it'd go in a separate case, a separate case.
A separate case, that's right. It's similar to these old-time baritone saxophone cases.
Do you remember how many times it folded? Did they fold it in half?
Just twice. Just one fold over. It was like you take a sheet of paper, like in a diamond shape.
Like so, like that.
Like so, like that. Just make one fold over, you see. Then you had all your rods and all. You had to put all that together.
Do you remember what the drum was made of?
It was sort of a lumen-like. Oh yeah. Like a metal. But it had no more calf heads. Normal calf skin heads, that's right. Two heads. Two heads. Normal calf skin heads.
How about the tuning stuff?
Well, the rods used to go, all that. He fixed, you know, you could call it collapsible drums.
Yeah.
After he put them and he'd add the rods and all that to it, it took a little time, you know, to rig them up.
But you've never seen anybody else with that.
He's the only one I've seen with that.
You know where he got that drum from?
No, I wouldn't know. Some say now he's out of Chicago. I wouldn't, I wouldn't, I would not, would not show about that, you know.
I guess you don't remember what make it was.
No, I really wouldn't know what make the drum it was. But he's the first I've seen with it.
Yeah.
Around in New Orleans.
About what time was he using this drum? Do you remember about the year?
That year, yeah. I remember that. That was around in, let's see, 23, 23. I was thinking about around 1925 like that. Yeah.
That was when he was playing with Piron?
Piron Band, that's the only one.
So he used that drum when he was playing with Piron?
Yeah, with Piron Band, yeah.
He used it on all of his jobs, did he?

Most likely, I wouldn't say all of them, but every time I seen him, he used it. Now, what did he ever use when he was working at Tranchina's nightclub, that old Spanish food? I don't know what kind of drums he's using out there, you know.
Do you remember what kind of cymbals he used at all, Louis Petron?
Zildjian.
Oh, Zildjian cymbals.
Zildjian cymbals, yeah.
Do you remember what kind of snare drum? I guess you don't remember that.
Well, I wouldn't remember the snare drum he used. No, it was... All I know, it was what you call them, they say, about a four-inch shell snare drum.
Do you remember anything about this guy, John McMurray?
John McMurray?
Yeah, he used to play on a single-headed snare drum, like a banjo hit.
Yeah, McMurray, let's see. I remember, yeah, John McMurray. Let's see. No, John... I heard lots about him. I remember John McMurray. I mean, I've seen him too much in person.
You tell me what this snare drum would be like. You ever seen a single-headed snare drum?
I'd never seen a single-headed snare drum, you know. It's actually being played by a single-headed snare drum.
You have no idea how there would be a single-head? Would it have the snare...
Well, I guess it would be similar to this... Like if I was to take this drum and just keep the batter aside and take the snare, it would be the same shell, you know.
Yeah, and put the snare underneath the batter, I guess.
That's all I could see. The only way you could... To get the vibration, to get the snare thick.
Yeah. Do you remember any other drummers, old drummers?
Yeah, no, let me see. It was like Mack Lacey. We had Mack Lacey, who was a good old drummer. We had Willigans.
Who was that?
Willigans. Oh, James Willigans. Willigans, yeah. You just played with Dumaine. Lacey Dumaine, that's right. And, well, you heard of Alfred William.
Yeah, Alfred William.
You heard of Abby Foster. You heard of Arthur Hogan.
Oh, was he playing in them days?
Yeah, he was playing. He used to call them Zongo, for nickname. Yeah? Like they called me, sorry, Zong. Everybody called him Zong.
What kind of stuff did he play?
He was a pretty fair drummer. He used to play a lot with Chris Kelly and them different bands. Then we had another one with my favorite in them days was Faso.
Oh, yeah.
I don't ever know his full name. I always called him Faso. Faso.
What kind of stuff did he play?
He was a good drummer.
Same kind of stuff like you were playing, right?
The drummer's similar to Happy, Red Happy.
Yeah.
Similar to Red Happy, Faso. He's similar to Red Happy. Fast drummer. He played with Chris Kelly Band, too.
Yeah?
And we had, let's see, well, you heard of Happy Goldstein.
Oh, yeah, Happy. He was playing in them days.
Yeah, he was playing in them days. Oh, yeah. Happy.
You remember a drummer called Two Bits?
Ernest Rapania.
Yeah.
He was called him nicknamed by Trap.
Oh, yeah, yeah. He was a bass drum player, essentially.
He played bass drum in a brass band. He played Trap drums, too. I was a drummer, yeah.
Do you remember what he played like? Was he a good drummer?
He was not a good drummer. He played with the Tuxedo Band years ago. What, Celestan's Tuxedo Band? Celestan's Baby Ridgely.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Yeah, he played as the original Tuxedo Band. He played with them bands.
You remember a drummer called Two Bits at all?
Two Bits?
Yeah.
Yeah, I heard a Missy. I heard some about him. That was his nickname.
Yeah, I don't know what his proper name was.
No, I heard lots about him. Two Bits. Let's see. Now, we had another drummer, I'm trying to think now. It was in my time. All these fellas that I'm relating to, there was, lots of them I came behind.
Yeah. Yeah.
That's all them drummers, I came behind them.
Yeah.
I used to look at some of them and play. But my two favorite drummers was, in them days was Happy.
Red Happy?
Red Happy and Willigan's.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah. I used to do lots of releases. After Willigan, he was playing drum. Mm-hmm. And he started wanting to send me on different jobs. Yeah. He liked the way I played, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, what kind of stuff did he play, James Willigan?

He was a drummer. He used to use plenty of roles. Like I said, the same, almost the same beats like Red Happy, James. Yeah. Want me to make some of them beats he makes? Yeah, sure. Yeah, beats he had to beat something like this.
Oh, yeah. Hey, would he use that on every tune, like Red Happy would use it?

Yeah, well, I figure some of them on most of every tune. You see, on exception of a slow number, well, a drummer, sometimes he's had it. Slow numbers always was hard on a man playing them. Yeah, yeah. Playing the drums. So when you get it, we used to call them bluesy tempos. Yeah, yeah. The day they called it, they got new names for them. We called them bluesy tempos. Well, I figure he played like I played them them days. Falling by honey, starlight. We played something like this. It's not too much of a flag to it. Oh, yeah. Well, one day. We had another one, too, with another fast drummer. It was called Black Benny.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Black Benny.
Remember what his name was?

I never know if Black Benny's right, full name, but I know he's played trap drums. We call them trap drums. It's orchestra drumming, and he was a bass drum player in the different brass bands around the city.
You ever play any parades in your early days?
I played lots of parades.
In the early days?
In the early days.
Did they play the same kind of stuff as they played?

It's mostly the same stuff you play in the day. Lots of funeral marches. I'll tell you how the bands did them days. Any band had a funeral march. They'd take the name of it, so the other band wouldn't know the name of it. Yeah, yeah. And the first man that started me on the parade was Ones Trapania, playing the parade. He played the bass drum, and I played the snare drum. That was part of the original tuxedo brass band.
Oh, yeah, yeah.

Yeah. Willie Paggio and Ones Trapania and myself. I think they had manual parades out that day. As long as we left a hall they called the New Hall on the street. They called North Durbin Street. It was many years ago. The first man brought me on a street parade.
How did you play in the old days in the dance bands? As much as you're playing today, the same sort of stuff?

Well, I never really changed my style of playing. I just tried to, except I played almost the same. I just always liked to, from Contrails, to listen to his style of playing, I always liked to dress a band with plenty of rolls on the snare drum. Because them days we didn't have a whole lot of tulip with tum-tums and plenty of cymbals, you see. So everything would depend on the bass and the snare drum. So I just tried to fill in a band with plenty of snare drum.
I guess that's like most of the drummers was doing the same thing.
Them days, yeah. You had the regular Chinese blocks, but everything depended on that snare drum.
Did you have any special beat?

No, just that beat I followed behind. That same beat I used to follow. And I changed that beat from that beat. This was my beat. Yeah. When I changed this beat, then I started following way back in the, I mean in later years, around in the late 30s. Yeah. That's why I started using this beat. It's called drag, thrush roll. Yeah. You know, like 30s. I first started using this beat when I was playing with Sidney Dees Vee in the band, around 1932 to 33. I called it the swing band. You know what I called it? It's called the thrush roll. Yeah. It's a thing.
I changed the band. You see. That was the style I played.
Yeah. Finally behind them swing bands. Changed it from that other beat from the olden days into that beat, around 1932 and 1933.
What was that beat that called Memphis Time? Was that just straight 4-4 beat?
Memphis Time, yeah. It was less than metal like this. You had another beat too. They used to make it like it was called an after beat.
Right. They just beat with one stick then. Yeah. Nice time. After beat.
Then they made that shuffle rhythm. In the late, early part to the 40s, they started using that shuffle rhythm.
Did they ever use drum solos in them days? You know, like Red Happy and them.

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah. Happy took solos. Yeah, he took solos when he wasn't in the show. He took drum solos. He made special breaks. And they used to feature them a whole lot in the Lyric Theater with whistles. Who, Happy? Red Happy, yeah. Plenty of drums. Plenty of drums.
What kind of drum solos would they take then? How many choruses?

You might take a chorus. A chorus. Well, one chorus or probably two, all the pens. That's what you call the overture, you know. Everybody used to put the spotlight on the drum and they just turn him loose. Then sometimes, too, they used to turn the drum as Chani Babay by himself.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah. I mean, sometimes turn drum solos on advertisements.
Oh, yeah.
Bands meet one there, you see. And then they either turn the drum loose or turn, you used to call the Big Four the rhythm session. That'd be the bass, the banjo, and the drum.
Yeah.

And whether it was a piano, if they used a piano like on a hall, well, the pianists call it the Big Four. They call it sticking the dogs on you. The bass balling, the drum, and the banjo. Sicking the dogs on you, the rhythm section, yeah.
Well, what kind of drum solos would they do? The same as now?
Yeah, well, it might be similar today because these drummers of the day, they make mostly paradiddles, you see.
Yeah.

But them guys made their drum solos with plenty of snare drum rolls and beats and then back to their four car bells and them rattles and all that. But the drummers of the day, they're making a whole lot of paradiddles beats, you know. I mean.
But, I mean, their drum solos would be sort of like those you did with Hammer's band.
Yeah. Mercy's band on Riverside. Yeah. That's one of the old-time drum solos, yeah.
You say you used to play these parades. You use the same drum as you've got here now?

Well, not this snare drum. I had another black. They both live. I had a black wood shell drum, similar to one like Happy Youth. And lots of parades in the later years, I used to use the same drum on his trapania used. Used to call it duplex snare drum. Oh, duplex. Me and Alfred used to alternate with the duplex snare drum, you see. We alternate on parades. If I go play a parade, he wouldn't be working with it. I get the snare drum from him.
Is that the one Alfred Williams got now, or is that a different one?
Well, I don't know. I don't know. It's the same duplex snare drum. I think it's the same drum on his trapania. I believe it's the same drum.
What drum you got there now?
This is a leader. Oh, leader, yeah. A leader snare here. Wood shell.
Yeah.
Metal hoop shell. That's a five bar. That's a six bar, a fourteen.
Yeah. It's got metal hoops and a wood shell.
Wood shell. Metal hoops, yeah.
How about the bass drum you have there? What's that? Slingland is it?
That's a Slingland bass, yeah.
And what about the cymbals?
I got this snare drum around 1947, like something like that. I love this drum here for a while.
Groomwald music still.
Yeah. Can you remember how much it cost in them days?
I just bought this drum separate. I paid 32 and a half for it. 32 and a half dollars. Yeah, 32 dollars. I bought it separate.
When was that, you said?
Around 47 or 46 something like that. 1947.
What cymbal do you use?
That's Zildjian.
Yeah, Zildjian.
Genuine cymbal. That cymbal is over 20 years old.
Yeah?
I have that cymbal over 20 years old.
It's got a pretty nice tone to it.
Genuine cymbal.
You want to do a little soft beating on that one, Andrew?
Yeah, that's a pretty nice tone.
That's 14. It's 14 and similar.
It's got a nice tone to it.
Yeah.
When did they start putting the dampers on these drums? Did they always have them on there?

No, we first started with cloths, using cloths on the bass drums. They killed the ringing sound effect of it when the band started improving. And now, well, I forgot what year these mutes came out. I really forgot what, but I know it's a pretty good ways back.
Yeah, yeah.
What exactly what you can't remember.
Is it, you think it spoils a tone on there?

No, no, it helps with a whole lot. It stops the drum from ringing a whole lot. You see, without that mute, here's a fake. You get, of course, this drum is still, I have that patent on it. But I'll give you a little idea, without that mute, with the sound, you see, with that patent. You know, just in the sound. And I still have a patent on there with that ball hitting on there.
Can we just put the mute on again and see how it sounds?

Tighten it up a little more, you see. All right, that's good right there. Okay. Okay. Keep that ringing effect off. Now, years ago, the drum couldn't ring enough. The more it'd ring, the more the band would like it.
The more they'd like it, yeah.
Yeah.
Big, that booming sound, didn't it?
Yeah, yeah. Let a bass drum ring, it goes right to the band's hand, you see, you could hear it from them. Good ways off.
You know, what are those things they call crowfoot pedals? You remember them? Crowfoot pedals? Yeah.

segments.title: Red Happy's single beat, seen in 1919
segments.summary: Frazier says Red Happy played the same beat on everything, even some blues numbers, and that he saw this in 1919.

segments.title: Robichaux band at the Old Lyric Theatre and Red Happy's departure
segments.summary: Frazier names the members of John Robichaux's band at the Lyric, the vaudeville repertoire, and says Red Happy left for Chicago.

segments.title: Red Happy's drum outfit and the bass drum cymbal beater
segments.summary: Frazier describes Happy's drum set and how the bass drum's side cymbal mechanism worked and could be released for soft passages.

segments.title: Chinee Foster and Louis Cottrell as snare drummers
segments.summary: Asked about other drummers, Frazier recalls Abbie 'Chinee' Foster of the original Tuxedo Band and names Louis Cottrell the best snare player, who also taught.

segments.title: Cottrell's collapsible bass drum
segments.summary: Frazier describes the folding bass drum, its case, heads and rigging, and that he saw only Cottrell use one.

segments.title: When Cottrell used the folding drum; his cymbals and snare
segments.summary: Around 1923-25 with the Piron band; Frazier recalls Zildjian cymbals and a four-inch shell snare.

segments.title: John McMurray and the single-headed snare drum
segments.summary: Allen asks about McMurray's single-headed snare; Frazier knows of him but never saw such a drum and speculates how it worked.

segments.title: Roll call of older drummers: Lacey, Willigan, Zongo, Faso, Goldston
segments.summary: Frazier lists drummers of earlier days and comments on Arthur Hogan, Faso (similar to Red Happy) and others.

segments.title: Ernest Trepagnier and the drummer called Two Bits
segments.summary: Frazier says Trepagnier played brass-band bass drum and traps but was not good; he had only heard of Two Bits.

segments.title: Frazier's favorites Red Happy and James Willigan; Black Benny
segments.summary: Frazier says he came after these drummers, favored Happy and Willigan, who sent him on jobs, and mentions Black Benny.

segments.title: Early street parades with the Tuxedo Brass Band
segments.summary: Frazier talks about funeral marches and being started on parades by Trepagnier in the original Tuxedo Brass Band.

segments.title: Frazier's style and the 1932-33 switch to the swing beat
segments.summary: He filled bands with snare rolls, then changed his beat to a thrush roll around 1932-33 with Sidney Desvigne, and describes other beats.

segments.title: Drum solos, the Big Four and old-time solos
segments.summary: Frazier describes solos by Red Happy and Chinee at the Lyric, the 'Big Four' rhythm section and how old solos differ from today's.

segments.title: Frazier's parade drums and present snare, bass drum and cymbal
segments.summary: He recalls the duplex snare shared with Alfred Williams, describes his current Leedy snare, Slingerland bass drum, price paid in 1947 and Zildjian cymbal.

segments.title: Bass drum mutes and the ringing sound
segments.summary: Cloths replaced by mutes to stop ringing; Frazier demonstrates, saying old bands liked a ringing bass drum; Allen asks about crowfoot pedals.
